title: The Dangers of Externalism
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Taking Warren Buffett's distinction between an Inner Scorecard and an Outer Scorecard, Stuart argues that teachers in an era of evaluation rubrics and data warehouses are pushed to define themselves by external measures. He grants the need for outside feedback but notes how easily observers can be fooled, pointing to formal evaluations as dog-and-pony shows that reward inauthentic performances. His central claim is that externalism does not yield optimal growth, whether for the valedictorian-chasing student, the rating-chasing teacher or the father fixated on successful kids. Because mental energy is finite, effort spent looking excellent cannot be spent becoming excellent. External validation is good, he concludes, but it makes a wretched top priority, and the best lives treat it as a side effect of an internal quest for excellence, as John Wooden did.
points: Stuart argues that current evaluation systems almost command teachers to define themselves by external measures, producing inauthentic performances on observation days.
Externalism undermines growth everywhere: grade-chasing students and rating-chasing teachers flourish less than those pursuing real excellence.
Because mental energy is finite, a teacher can obsess about being great or about looking great, but not both.
External validation is good but should be a side effect of an internal quest for excellence, as in John Wooden's definition of success.
His practical advice is to spend less time on evaluation rubrics and more on good books, smart people and thinking about great teaching.
quotes: In our era of complex teacher evaluation systems, book-length observation rubrics, and “data warehouses,” you and I are almost commanded to define ourselves by external measures. While I certainly accept the ease with which I can deceive myself (and therefore the need for external feedback on how I'm teaching or living), I am equally aware of the ease with which I can fool most people into thinking I'm better at things than I actually am.

This, by the way, is what the system is presently destined to create: inauthentic performances where teachers teach how they think they are supposed to teach so that they can get a teacher evaluation score that means they get to keep their job.
The teacher driven simply to get a Highly Effective evaluation score is unlikely to flourish as much long-term as the teacher driven simply to be as excellent as he can be at his calling.

Why do I think these things are true? We're finite creatures with finite mental energies. Effort expended on attaining a five out of five on element 3.E.w of the Ninety-Two Dimensions of Great Teaching rubric is effort that cannot be expended thinking or reading deeply about what assessment is good for.
You can obsess about being a great teacher, or about looking like one — you can't obsess about both.

The thing is, external validation isn't ultimate; it makes a wretched Top Priority and a horrible god. Again and again, it seems like the people who live the best lives and do the most important work are those for whom external validation is a side effect of an internal quest for excellence.
Spend less time reading your teacher eval rubric and more time reading good books, talking to smart people, and thinking about great teaching.
